trial_name: APROCCHSS — Hydrocortisone plus Fludrocortisone for Adults with Septic Shock (2018)
citation: Annane D, Renault A, Brun-Buisson C, et al. Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone for adults with septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(9):809-818
one_liner: In adults with septic shock, hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduced 90-day mortality (43% vs 49%, RR 0.88) and accelerated shock reversal.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with persistent septic shock requiring vasopressors despite fluid resuscitation, within 24 hours of shock onset
pico.intervention: Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h + fludrocortisone 50 mcg daily for 7 days

background.existing_knowledge: Septic shock remains a leading cause of ICU death; corticosteroids had long been used to accelerate shock reversal, but mortality effects were uncertain and trial results conflicted.
background.knowledge_gap: A prior RCT of low-dose hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone suggested improved survival, whereas a later large trial of hydrocortisone alone did not show mortality benefit and raised questions around testing/targeting 'relative adrenal insufficiency'.
background.hypothesis: In adults with persistent septic shock, adjunctive low-dose corticosteroid therapy (hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone) would reduce all-cause 90-day mortality compared with placebo, while also hastening resolution of cardiovascular and organ failure.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; initially a 2×2 factorial with drotrecogin alfa, later continued as a two-group corticosteroid trial after drotrecogin withdrawal.

inclusion: Suspected/confirmed infection with shock requiring vasopressors despite fluid resuscitation
Randomisation within 24 hours of shock onset
High illness severity (SAPS II ~56, ~92% mechanically ventilated, ~27–28% on renal-replacement therapy at baseline)
exclusion: Other protocol-defined conditions (including bleeding contraindications during the original factorial design)

methods.intervention: Hydrocortisone hemisuccinate 50 mg IV every 6 hours (200 mg/day) for 7 days + Fludrocortisone 50 micrograms once daily (oral/NG) for 7 days.
methods.comparison: Matched IV placebo injections every 6 hours plus matched oral/NG placebo tablets daily for 7 days.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors); placebo formulations matched active drugs.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 1280 patients to detect a 10% absolute reduction in 90-day mortality (from 45% to 35%) with 95% power at a two-sided 5% significance level; achieved 1241 (97% of target).

headline_bullets: Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduced 90-day mortality (43.0% vs 49.1%; RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.78–0.99; P=0.03) and was directionally consistent across multiple mortality timepoints.
The regimen accelerated shock recovery (vasopressor-free days to day 28: 17.8 ± 10.4 vs 15.0 ± 11.1; P<0.001) and increased organ-failure–free days (14.8 ± 11.5 vs 13.6 ± 11.9; P=0.003).
Expected metabolic harms were observed (hyperglycaemia 89.1% vs 82.3%; RR 1.07; 95% CI 1.03–1.12; P=0.002), without clear increases in gastroduodenal bleeding or superinfection in reported endpoints.

outcomes_table.note: Primary comparison after continuation as two-group corticosteroid trial.
Numerical reduction; not statistically significant at 5%.
Small attrition by day 180 (denominators < randomised N).

outcomes_table.outcome: Decision to withhold/withdraw active treatment by day 90
outcomes_table.note: Potentially both a mediator and an outcome influenced by clinical trajectory.
Mean ± SD; indicates faster cardiovascular recovery.
Also more days with blood glucose ≥150 mg/dL: 4.3 ± 4.1 vs 3.4 ± 3.8; P<0.001.
No signal for excess GI bleeding with steroids in this cohort.
Definition per trial report; interpret alongside antimicrobial stewardship context.
Non-significant trend; ascertainment depends on survival and follow-up.

subgroup_table.note: Targeted analysis of APROCCHSS participants; suggests potential effect heterogeneity by infection phenotype.

safety: Hyperglycaemia: 89.1% vs 82.3% (RR 1.07, P=0.002); more days with glucose ≥150 mg/dL (4.3 vs 3.4 days, P<0.001).
Neurologic sequelae (MDRS >1) by day 180: 24.9% vs 20.8% (RR 1.20, P=0.08).

domains.notes: Central randomisation with permuted blocks (size 8), stratification by ICU; allocation concealment maintained through identical placebo preparations and blinded dispensing.
Double-blind (patients, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors); placebo formulations matched active drugs; primary endpoint (mortality) is objective.
Primary endpoint ascertainment robust; day 180 attrition small (611/614 and 625/627), unlikely to overturn effect estimates but relevant to disability/neurologic outcomes.
Biological separation evident via metabolic effects (days with glucose ≥150 mg/dL: 4.3 vs 3.4; P<0.001) and physiological response (vasopressor-free days: 17.8 vs 15.0; P<0.001).
Groups clinically similar at baseline (mechanical ventilation 92.3% vs 91.3%; RRT 27.0% vs 28.1%; norepinephrine-equivalent dose ~1.02 vs 1.14 µg/kg/min; SAPS II ~56 ± 19).

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears strong for the primary mortality endpoint given concealed randomisation, blinding, and objective outcome assessment, with moderate caution warranted for secondary/discharge-dependent outcomes and for interpretive complexity introduced by trial interruptions and design evolution.

domains.notes: Enrolled patients were severely ill (high vasopressor dose; ~92% ventilated), aligning with typical ICU septic shock populations in high-income settings, but may over-represent more severe shock compared with mixed ED/ward cohorts.

Conducted in French ICUs with structured sepsis management and access to vasopressors, ventilation, and renal replacement; transferability to resource-limited settings depends on availability of close glucose monitoring, vasopressor titration, and fludrocortisone formulations.
Hydrocortisone bolus dosing is widely feasible; adding daily fludrocortisone requires enteral access and supply, and is not a universal component of sepsis protocols.

Subsequent analyses suggest potential effect heterogeneity by infection phenotype (e.g., community-acquired pneumonia-related septic shock), supporting cautious extrapolation beyond the dominant phenotypes enrolled.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is good to adult ICU septic shock in comparable high-resource systems, but is less certain in lower-acuity sepsis populations, settings without routine enteral drug delivery/monitoring capacity, and phenotypes where treatment effect may differ.

limitations: Complex trial history (initial factorial design, discontinuation of one intervention component, enrolment interruptions)
Near-but-not-complete achievement of planned sample size
Extensive secondary outcomes without multiplicity adjustment
Discharge-related endpoints influenced by centre practice
Limited direct evidence within the trial to isolate the incremental contribution of fludrocortisone versus hydrocortisone alone

critical_appraisal.summary: APROCCHSS is a well-conducted RCT with strong internal validity for its primary mortality endpoint, demonstrating a modest but clinically relevant mortality reduction with hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone in severe septic shock; generalisability is good to similar ICU settings, though the incremental benefit of fludrocortisone remains uncertain.
weaknesses: Secondary outcomes not adjusted for multiplicity
Discharge-related outcomes influenced by centre practice

sections.authors_conclusion: In severe septic shock with ongoing vasopressor dependence, a 7-day regimen of hydrocortisone (200 mg/day in divided doses) plus fludrocortisone (50 micrograms/day) provides evidence of a modest but clinically relevant mortality reduction and faster haemodynamic recovery.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: In adults with septic shock requiring vasopressors, adding hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h plus fludrocortisone 50 mcg daily for 7 days reduces 90-day mortality and accelerates shock resolution.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: ICU patients with severe septic shock, within 24 hours of onset, in settings with enteral access and glucose monitoring.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean that hydrocortisone alone is ineffective; the trial cannot separate the effect of fludrocortisone.
implementation_caveats: Consider potential heterogeneity by infection phenotype

controversies.topic: Trial evolution as a validity stress-test
controversies.notes: The protocol’s transition from a factorial design to a two-group corticosteroid trial, plus recruitment suspensions and near-target (not complete) sample size, complicate causal storytelling but do not negate the randomised comparison within the final corticosteroid phase.

APROCCHSS demonstrated a statistically significant 90-day mortality reduction with hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone, while ADRENAL (hydrocortisone infusion without routine fludrocortisone) did not show a mortality benefit, although it improved shock resolution and ICU processes. Earlier CORTICUS found no mortality benefit and revived concerns about patient selection, timing, and adrenal testing paradigms.

controversies.topic: Role of fludrocortisone remains an evidence gap
controversies.notes: APROCCHSS cannot disentangle whether benefit stems from hydrocortisone dosing strategy, fludrocortisone addition, or both; no large head-to-head RCT has definitively compared hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone versus hydrocortisone alone using mortality as a primary endpoint.

controversies.topic: Contemporary synthesis of the totality of evidence
controversies.notes: A patient-level meta-analysis of IV hydrocortisone trials (excluding the routine mineralocorticoid component) found no mortality reduction, while showing a modest increase in vasopressor-free days (mean difference 1.24 days; 95% CI 0.74 to 1.73) and specific adverse effects such as hypernatraemia and muscle weakness.

A Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing placebo/usual care, hydrocortisone alone, and hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone suggested lower mortality with hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone versus placebo (RR 0.85; 95% CrI 0.72 to 0.99) and a non-definitive difference versus hydrocortisone alone (RR 0.88; 95% CrI 0.74 to 1.03), highlighting ongoing uncertainty about incremental benefit over hydrocortisone monotherapy.

In a targeted analysis of APROCCHSS participants with community-acquired pneumonia-related septic shock, hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone was associated with lower 90-day mortality (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.83), raising the possibility of clinically meaningful heterogeneity by infection source/phenotype.

A retrospective target-trial emulation in routine practice compared hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone against hydrocortisone alone and reported lower in-hospital mortality with combination therapy, supporting plausibility but remaining vulnerable to residual confounding and treatment-selection bias.

The paired 2018 NEJM steroid trials prompted editorial emphasis on careful interpretation of ‘borderline’ mortality findings, co-interventions, and regimen differences, alongside formal correspondence debating whether fludrocortisone explains divergent trial outcomes and whether hydrocortisone trial designs were sufficiently comparable.

Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 conditionally recommends corticosteroids for septic shock with ongoing vasopressor requirement (commonly hydrocortisone 200 mg/day), without mandating mineralocorticoid co-therapy. A 2024 focused update similarly issued a conditional recommendation for corticosteroids in septic shock and recommended against high-dose/short-duration regimens.

The most recent Cochrane update concludes that corticosteroids probably reduce short- and longer-term mortality in sepsis overall, while uncertainties persist for optimal dosing strategy and adverse effects, which frames APROCCHSS as part of a broader, evolving evidence base rather than a standalone ‘final answer’.

context_related_trials.relation: Hydrocortisone infusion without routine fludrocortisone did not show mortality benefit but improved shock resolution; contrasts with APROCCHSS mortality finding.
Earlier trial of hydrocortisone without fludrocortisone found no mortality benefit and raised concerns about patient selection and adrenal testing.

unresolved_questions: Does fludrocortisone add incremental mortality benefit over hydrocortisone alone?
Is the treatment effect consistent across all infection phenotypes?
What is the optimal corticosteroid regimen (dose, duration, mineralocorticoid) in septic shock?
How do these findings apply to lower-acuity sepsis or resource-limited settings?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In severe septic shock, a 7-day course of hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduces 90-day mortality and speeds shock reversal, with hyperglycaemia as the main trade-off.
